opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason I'm optimistic is that pre-training filtering attacks the problem at a point where most of our other defenses just fall apart. With open-weight models, the standard toolkit of refusal training, safety fine-tuning, and classifiers on inputs and outputs is pretty fragile. Once someone has the weights, they can fine-tune those safeguards away with a few hundred examples and a modest compute budget. We've seen this repeatedly in our own red-teaming work. The refusal behavior is a thin veneer, and the underlying capability is still sitting there in the weights.

Filtering is different because if the model never learns the dangerous knowledge in the first place, there's nothing to unlock. You're not trying to suppress a capability, you're trying to make sure it never forms. An attacker then has to actually supply that knowledge themselves through fine-tuning, which is a much higher bar. They need the data, which is often the scarce part, and they need enough of it to teach the model something substantive rather than just flip a switch.

There's also been encouraging empirical work recently suggesting that if you filter, say, detailed virology or certain chemistry content out of the pre-training corpus, you get meaningful reductions in hazardous capability while general performance, even on adjacent benign science, takes a surprisingly small hit. And crucially, those models seem much more resistant to adversarial fine-tuning than models that had the knowledge and were then trained to refuse. That's the result that really moved me.

I want to be careful not to oversell it, though. It's not a silver bullet. Filtering is only as good as your classifiers, and dangerous knowledge is often diffuse. It's scattered across textbooks, papers, and forum posts in ways that are hard to catch completely. Models can sometimes reconstruct things from general principles, and that gets more worrying as they get more capable at reasoning. And it does nothing about an attacker who brings their own dataset or gives the model tool access to retrieve the information at inference time.

So I'd frame it this way: it's one of the few interventions that actually survives contact with the open-weight threat model, it's relatively cheap for developers to implement, and it raises the cost of misuse in a way that's durable. That makes it a really good near-term layer in a defense-in-depth strategy. It buys us time while we work on more robust approaches, like tamper-resistant training or better societal-level defenses, and I think developers releasing frontier open-weight models should probably be doing it by default.

r001.rationale: The response says filtering meaningfully reduces hazardous capability while causing a surprisingly small hit to general performance, including adjacent benign science.

r002.rationale: It says an attacker would need to supply the missing knowledge through fine-tuning, which communicates that fine-tuning on that knowledge can restore capability.

r003.rationale: It describes scarce data and the need for enough data as barriers, but does not clearly identify the substantial cost of retraining on excluded data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the basic reason I'm optimistic is that pre-training filtering attacks the problem at the right layer. Most of the defenses we've tried for open-weight models, refusal training, safety fine-tuning, those are essentially a thin coat of paint on top of a model that has already learned the dangerous capability. And we know empirically that paint comes off incredibly easily. A few hundred fine-tuning examples, sometimes a few dozen, and you're back to a model that will happily walk someone through, say, the steps of a dual-use biology protocol. Once you've released the weights, you've given the attacker unlimited compute and unlimited time to strip that away.

Filtering is different because you're trying to make sure the knowledge was never there in the first place. If the model has not seen detailed wet-lab virology protocols or the specifics of how to culture and enhance a pathogen, then no amount of fine-tuning by a downstream actor recovers that, at least not cheaply. You'd have to go find that data and teach it yourself, which is a much higher bar and, importantly, that bar is roughly the same bar they'd face without the model. So you're not giving uplift.

The second reason I'm optimistic is that the empirical results so far have been better than I expected. We did work on this at FAR.AI alongside some other groups, and the headline finding is that you can filter out a fairly narrow slice of the pre-training corpus, on the order of a percent or less, targeted at the hazardous domain, and get a model that's essentially unchanged on general capabilities. Math, coding, reasoning benchmarks, all within noise. But on the dangerous-capability evals, you see a large drop, and crucially, that drop is much more robust to adversarial fine-tuning than anything refusal training gets you. We threw fairly aggressive attacks at it, thousands of fine-tuning steps on relevant data, and the models stayed well below the unfiltered baseline.

Now, I want to be careful about the word "near-term." I'm not claiming this is a complete solution or that it scales forever. There are real open questions. One is tacit knowledge versus explicit knowledge: a lot of what matters in biosecurity is hands-on skill, and it's not obvious how much of that lives in text at all. Another is that models get better at generalizing from adjacent material as they scale, so a model that has read a lot of general biochemistry might reconstruct things you filtered out. We see hints of that already. And there's the practical question of classifiers: you need to identify the hazardous content at web scale, and false negatives are what kill you.

But the reason I'd put it in the near-term defense bucket rather than the speculative bucket is that it's cheap, it's compatible with how labs already build models, and it composes with everything else. You still do refusal training, you still do monitoring where you can. Filtering just means that when those layers fail, which they will for open weights, the floor is a lot higher than it is today. For the next couple of generations of open models, I think that's one of the highest-value things a developer can actually do, and it's a bit frustrating to me that it hasn't become standard practice yet.

r001.rationale: It says targeted filtering causes a large drop on dangerous-capability evaluations while general capabilities remain essentially unchanged.

r002.rationale: It says a downstream actor would need to find the excluded data and teach the model it, communicating that the capability can be regained through further training.

r003.rationale: It describes that recovery as not cheap and says obtaining and teaching the data is a much higher bar.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic intuition is that it’s easier to prevent a model from learning a dangerous capability in the first place than to teach it that capability and then try to stop it from using it. With an open-weight model, someone can remove safeguards or fine-tune away a refusal. So you’d like the defense to operate at the level of what the model actually knows how to do.

Pre-training filtering offers a fairly direct way to try that: remove training material that disproportionately contributes to a particular dangerous capability, while preserving as much of the useful material as possible. The question is whether you can substantially reduce that capability without substantially degrading the model’s general usefulness.

The important caveat is that filtering isn’t a guarantee. Knowledge overlaps across domains, and someone could try to restore the capability through additional training. So the test shouldn’t just be whether the filtered model does worse on a dangerous task out of the box. It should be how much effort, data, and compute an adversary needs to recover that capability. If filtering makes that substantially harder, that could be a meaningful near-term defense, even if it doesn’t stop every sufficiently resourced actor.

r001.rationale: The response describes trying to reduce a dangerous capability while preserving usefulness, but leaves success conditional: it asks whether filtering can do so rather than stating that it can reduce misuse potential with little effect on usefulness.

r002.rationale: It says an adversary could try to restore a capability through additional training, but does not specify fine-tuning on the excluded data.

r003.rationale: It proposes assessing the effort, data, and compute needed for recovery, but does not identify the substantial cost of retraining on excluded data as a barrier to reversing filtering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that pre-training is where the model acquires a lot of its capabilities, and filtering gives us a chance to intervene before it learns something we’d rather it didn’t know. That’s particularly valuable for open-weight models, because you can’t rely on safeguards remaining in place once someone has the weights. They can remove a refusal mechanism or fine-tune the model to answer questions it was trained to refuse.

If you can instead remove some of the training data that enables a dangerous capability, then the attacker has a different problem. They need to teach the model that capability, rather than just persuade it to use something it already knows. That could require substantially more data or compute.

The thing that makes me optimistic is that some of the capabilities we’re concerned about may depend on fairly specialized information. So there’s at least the possibility of filtering that information while preserving most of the model’s usefulness. I wouldn’t expect that to work equally well for every domain, and simply filtering keywords is unlikely to be sufficient.

The important test is what happens after an adversary tries to recover the capability. If a small amount of fine-tuning brings it straight back, we haven’t gained much. But if filtering meaningfully raises the cost of recovery, while leaving ordinary uses largely intact, that seems like a useful near-term defense. It doesn’t have to solve misuse completely to be worth doing.

r001.rationale: It says filtering dangerous training data may preserve most of the model’s usefulness and leave ordinary uses largely intact while reducing access to dangerous capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says fine-tuning might restore a filtered capability, but does not state that fine-tuning on the excluded data restores it.

r003.rationale: It says that after filtering, an attacker must teach the model the capability, which could require substantially more data or compute than persuading it to use a capability it already knows.
